case.case_title: Bandara and Others v. Jagoda Arachchi, Officer in Charge, Police Station, Fort and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application Nos. 687/97-690/97, decided on 9 February 2000

clause.text: Freedom of speech and expression including publication.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the police action in dispersing the picketing university students infringed their fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 14(1)(a).
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioners argued that their freedom of speech and expression was infringed when the police dispersed their peaceful picketing campaign protesting educational reforms.
case_context.respondent_argument: The police contended that the dispersal was lawful to prevent breach of public peace as the protesters became unruly, obstructed traffic, and caused damage, thus justifying restrictions under Article 15(7).
key_facts: University students organized a picketing campaign protesting government educational reforms.
Over 3000 persons assembled outside Fort Railway Station displaying placards.
Protesters moved onto the main road causing obstruction and congestion.
Police ordered dispersal and used tear gas, batons, and water cannon after protesters did not comply.
Some protesters caused damage to shops and injured police officers.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court held that the freedom of speech and expression under Article 14(1)(a) is not absolute and is subject to restrictions in the interest of public order as provided by Article 15(7). Peaceful expression is protected, but when the conduct leads to breach of peace or public order, restrictions are justified.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The court found that the initial picketing was a lawful exercise of freedom of speech and expression. However, when the protesters obstructed the road and caused damage, the police acted lawfully under statutory powers to disperse the assembly, thus not infringing the petitioners' fundamental rights.
principles_established: Freedom of speech and expression includes peaceful protest but is subject to reasonable restrictions for public order.
The right is not limited to matters of immediate personal concern but extends to public issues.
Police have lawful authority to disperse assemblies that cease to be peaceful and cause public disorder.
precedents_cited: Bernard Zoysa v. The Attorney General (1991) 2 Sri L.R. 56
Hague, Mayor et al vs Committee for Industrial Organisation 307 US 496

outcome.holding: The court dismissed the petitioners' claim, holding that the police action did not infringe their fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 14(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression, which the petitioners claimed was infringed by police dispersal. The court's reasoning centered on interpreting this clause's scope and permissible restrictions, making it central to the decision.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The court held that the placards and protest constituted an exercise of freedom of speech and expression, but the police acted lawfully when dispersing the assembly after it ceased to be peaceful and obstructed traffic.
